title: GlacierBank x Redwood — Private deployment day-2 ops (audit logs, incident diagnostics, SLO reporting)

GlacierBank emphasized regulated controls: immutable audit trails, SIEM forwarding, separation of duties, and deterministic runbooks for on-call. Next steps: Redwood to share sample audit events schema, SLO export formats, and a proposed architecture diagram for GlacierBank’s private control plane + logging pipeline; GlacierBank to confirm target SIEM, retention windows, and required RBAC roles for go-live.

transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: GlacierBank x Redwood — Private deployment day-2 ops (audit logs, incident diagnostics, SLO reporting)
Date: 2025-04-02
Time: 2:00pm–2:52pm ET
Duration: 52 minutes
Call type: Technical deep dive

Attendees:
- Neha Kapoor (Redwood, AE)
- Dylan Brooks (Redwood, Bot/Tooling)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood, Security/Compliance)
- Kevin Osei (Redwood, Audit Logging)
- Chloe Martin (Redwood, Console)
- Elena Markovic (GlacierBank, Platform Eng)
- Greg Han (GlacierBank, SRE)
- Priya Desai (GlacierBank, InfoSec)
- Marcus Reed (GlacierBank, GRC)
- Nina Alvarez (GlacierBank, ML Platform)

---

[00:00] Neha Kapoor: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is day-two ops for Redwood Private. So audit logs, incident diagnostics, and SLO reporting—like what you actually live with at 2 a.m.

[00:18] Elena Markovic: Yes. Exactly. We have the feature checklist, but the ops and control story is where deals go to die for us, so—sorry—just being blunt.

[00:27] Neha Kapoor: No, totally fair. We brought Kevin and Naomi specifically so you can go deep on that.

[00:35] Greg Han: For context, our on-call is pretty strict. If the system is on fire, the tools cannot add load, and we need deterministic runbooks. Also audit, always.

[00:47] Dylan Brooks: Yep. That’s basically what we’ve been building internally as well. For Private, we try to keep the “diagnostics collector” bounded—timeouts, caching, and it degrades to links when the live queries are expensive or failing.

[01:02] Priya Desai: Before we jump to bots, can you anchor the topology? In a private VPC deployment, what exactly is in our network versus yours? Like control plane vs data plane.

[01:13] Naomi Feldman: Sure. The usual pattern is: the inference data plane—model serving and request handling—runs inside your VPC under your networking controls. The control plane can be either private as well, or a split model with an on-prem-ish management plane. For regulated customers, we generally do a customer-managed networking model. We’ll follow up with the exact diagram for your target.

[01:35] Elena Markovic: We’re assuming “no public endpoints.” Any exception requires a security review. We can do private link / VPN, but… not random egress.

[01:46] Chloe Martin: Understood. For Console deep links, it’s basically just URLs into the private Console instance. Nothing needs to traverse the public internet if you host the UI internally.

[01:58] Marcus Reed: And the audit logs—those have to end up in Splunk, immutable. We have retention requirements.

[02:07] Kevin Osei: Great. On audit: we emit audit events for privileged actions and reads. Examples: “config diff requested,” “telemetry query executed via diagnostics,” “role/scope changed,” “break-glass grant used,” “admin changed routing policy,” and so on. Those events can be forwarded to Splunk via HEC or to whatever SIEM pipeline you have. In Private, you can run the forwarder locally.

[02:32] Greg Han: When you say “telemetry query executed,” do you mean every single query a human runs? Or only what the bot runs?

[02:39] Kevin Osei: Both are possible depending on how you wire it. For the incident diagnostics tools specifically, we audit the bot identity and the request context—incident id, channel/thread id if it’s Slack, time window, and which datasource it hit. For human-driven queries, if you route them through the same gateway, yes you get audit.

[03:02] Priya Desai: We’d want that. At minimum for privileged endpoints and config reads.

[03:09] Naomi Feldman: That matches our default. Least privilege with explicit scopes.

[03:14] Elena Markovic: Okay. Now talk about incident diagnostics. You’re referencing a bot. We’re not married to Slack, but our responders live in ServiceNow and Teams. So—how portable is the concept?

[03:27] Dylan Brooks: The “incident bot” thing is basically a UI on top of a diagnostics payload. Internally we render it as Slack cards, but the payload is generic: recent deploy context, config diffs (redacted), and saturation signals. For Private, you could integrate with Teams, or you could push into your incident ticket template.

[03:46] Nina Alvarez: Can you list the actual signals? Like if I’m debugging latency spikes on a private cluster.

[03:52] Dylan Brooks: Yep. Common ones:
- Deploy timeline: service name, version/image SHA, rollout phase, whether canary is healthy.
- Config diffs: feature flags, routing policy changes, quota/rate limit changes, model pin changes.
- Saturation: GPU utilization, queue depth, scheduler backpressure/admission control, KV cache pressure.
And then links: dashboards, traces, logs.

[04:20] Greg Han: “KV cache pressure”—are you measuring evictions? Or some percent?

[04:25] Dylan Brooks: Both. Different runtimes report different primitives. But the card surfaces something actionable like “high cache churn / eviction rate” plus a trend.

[04:35] Greg Han: I like that. Most vendors just say “GPU is high” which is not helpful.

[04:41] Elena Markovic: But the bank question: is any of that tenant-aware? In our case it’s internal business units. But still, we separate environments.

[04:50] Naomi Feldman: The redaction story is mainly about not leaking secrets and not over-sharing across tenants. For your private deployment, you still want redaction because people paste screenshots, and also because your separation-of-duties policy may require it. You can enforce allowlists on config fields. Anything that matches secret patterns is masked.

[05:12] Priya Desai: I need specifics. If a config diff shows KMS key IDs, tokens, endpoints—how do you guarantee it doesn’t show up in a Teams message or whatever.

[05:23] Dylan Brooks: We treat config diffs as sensitive. The safe mode is: show only allowlisted keys + redacted values. We also do pattern-based redaction for anything that looks like secret material. And we have tests that fail if those show up in rendered output.

[05:42] Marcus Reed: And auditing. If someone expands a diff, I want an event.

[05:47] Kevin Osei: Yes. “ConfigDiffViewed” is an event. It includes who, when, and the scope—service, env, time range.

[05:58] Chloe Martin: Also, in the UI we can show “redacted fields hidden” banners, so responders know they’re not seeing everything.

[06:06] Greg Han: Okay, but incident time—break-glass. We do have a break-glass process. How does yours work?

[06:15] Naomi Feldman: Our pattern: normal on-call role can view safe diffs and standard telemetry. For Sev0/Sev1, you can request a temporary elevated scope, time-boxed, with mandatory reason. That emits audit events. Then it auto-expires.

[06:33] Priya Desai: Who can grant it?

[06:35] Naomi Feldman: In Private, that can be your own approver group. Typically security + SRE leads. We don’t want Redwood staff having to approve access in your environment.

[06:47] Elena Markovic: Good.

[06:49] Greg Han: Back to load. We’ve had issues where “helpful diagnostics” hammer metrics backends during incidents. What are your guardrails?

[06:58] Dylan Brooks: This is a big one. Guardrails:
1) Query budgets: fixed time window defaults (like last 15 minutes), bounded label cardinality.
2) Timeouts and retries: short timeout, one retry, then degrade.
3) Caching and request coalescing: if five people click “refresh,” we do one query.
4) Load shedding: if error rates are high or the telemetry backend is slow, we stop doing live queries and return cached context + links.

[07:29] Greg Han: That’s exactly what I wanted to hear.

[07:31] Nina Alvarez: What about model-specific stuff like batch size or quantization changes—does that show up in deploy context?

[07:39] Dylan Brooks: If it’s controlled via config, it would show up as config diff. If it’s baked into the image, it shows up as deploy version and you can link to the PR or commit.

[07:51] Elena Markovic: Wait, link to PR—so you’re assuming GitHub access.

[07:55] Neha Kapoor: In your environment, that would link to your internal repo if you want. Internally, our bot links to GitHub PRs. But it’s configurable.

[08:06] Chloe Martin: The link generator is templated. It can point to GitHub Enterprise or whatever you use.

[08:12] Marcus Reed: We’d need that validated. No links to public GitHub.

[08:15] Chloe Martin: Totally. We’ll note it.

[08:20] Priya Desai: SLO reporting—how do you do it? We have SLOs for latency and availability. We want burn rate alerts and weekly reporting.

[08:31] Chloe Martin: We support SLO definitions per service/route/region. You can view error budget burn in Console. There are deep links for “last 1h, 6h, 24h” burn. For export, there are options—links, JSON snapshots, and you can scrape metrics into your existing Grafana.

[08:53] Greg Han: We use Grafana + Prometheus and then ServiceNow for incidents.

[08:57] Chloe Martin: Perfect. We can map SLOs to Prometheus queries. We’ll share a sample.

[09:04] Kevin Osei: On audit again: viewing SLO dashboards is generally not privileged, but changing SLO definitions is. That’s audited.

[09:14] Marcus Reed: Do you support retention policies? Like, audit logs 400 days. Metrics maybe 30 days. Traces 7 days.

[09:22] Kevin Osei: Yes. The audit log retention depends on your storage. We can configure retention and also forward to your centralized system. In regulated environments, we recommend forwarding to your WORM-compliant store.

[09:39] Priya Desai: Who signs those logs? Like, how do we know they weren’t tampered with.

[09:45] Kevin Osei: We can add integrity controls—at minimum, ship to your immutable store. If you need cryptographic signing, we can discuss; it depends on your policy.

[09:57] Elena Markovic: Let’s capture that as an open requirement. It may be needed.

[10:03] Neha Kapoor: Noted.

[10:06] Nina Alvarez: What does “incident context” look like without Slack? Sorry, I keep coming back. If we use Teams, can we get the same cards?

[10:16] Dylan Brooks: The payload is JSON. The “cards” are just a view. We can render adaptive cards for Teams, or you can ingest into your own incident record. The key is the schema: deploys, config diff summary, saturation summary, and links.

[10:38] Greg Han: And if the telemetry backend is down, you still can provide deploy and config?

[10:43] Dylan Brooks: Usually yes, because deploy metadata and config store are different systems. But if config service is unhealthy, then we fall back to “last known diff” and manual steps.

[10:55] Greg Han: “Manual steps” is important. Give me the command to run.

[10:58] Dylan Brooks: Yep. In degraded mode we add a snippet: “If card is empty, run X” and link to the runbook.

[11:10] Priya Desai: Permissioning. The bot identity—does it have broad read access?

[11:15] Naomi Feldman: No. It has explicit scopes: deploy metadata read, safe config diff read, telemetry query read for bounded metrics. Anything beyond that requires break-glass.

[11:31] Marcus Reed: And the audit event includes what scope was used.

[11:34] Kevin Osei: Exactly.

[11:36] Elena Markovic: Alright. Can we go through a hypothetical? Let’s say latency spikes in eu-west, 503s increase.

[11:44] Dylan Brooks: Sure. First five minutes context would show:
- Recent deploys in eu-west for the gateway / scheduler / serving service.
- Any routing policy changes, quota changes.
- Saturation: queue depth rising, GPU at 92%, backpressure toggled on, KV cache eviction high.
Then it would recommend: check error budget burn link, open saturation dashboard, look at traces.

[12:12] Greg Han: That “recommend” part—is it deterministic? Like, we don’t want an LLM hallucinating actions.

[12:18] Dylan Brooks: Great callout. We keep it rules-based. No generative suggestions in the critical path. It’s basically “if signals A+B then show runbook link.”

[12:31] Greg Han: Love it.

[12:34] Nina Alvarez: What about model fallback routing? If capacity is tight, does it route to smaller model? And is that visible?

[12:43] Chloe Martin: Yes. Routing and fallback policies are config. So diffs would show if someone changed fallback thresholds. And the diagnostics can show “fallback rate” as a metric, but we’re careful on cardinality.

[12:57] Greg Han: Cardinality is a killer.

[13:00] Chloe Martin: Exactly. We aggregate by service/region, not by request id.

[13:06] Priya Desai: Competitor question. We’ve looked at Bedrock and Azure OpenAI. Their ops story is—opaque. You’re saying we can have full observability in our VPC.

[13:18] Neha Kapoor: That’s the thesis of Private. You get the knobs and the visibility, but you’re not building the whole inference stack.

[13:27] Elena Markovic: Okay but then responsibility boundary: who is on-call for what? If the control plane component breaks, do we page you?

[13:36] Neha Kapoor: For Private, we usually have a support SLA and escalation path. Your team owns your environment, but we provide support and can help diagnose. The key is: our tooling needs to provide you enough context without requiring Redwood engineers to have privileged access.

[13:57] Priya Desai: Thank you.

[14:00] Marcus Reed: Also, evidence for auditors. We need to show: change management, access logs, incident records with timestamps.

[14:09] Kevin Osei: We can export an incident timeline format—basically a structured timeline that includes deploy events, config changes, and who ran diagnostics. That’s useful for postmortems and audits.

[14:25] Greg Han: Is that export manual or automatic?

[14:28] Kevin Osei: Can be automatic when an incident is created. Or manual via API.

[14:35] Elena Markovic: That’s useful.

[14:38] Nina Alvarez: How does model versioning work? Are we pinning model artifact hashes?

[14:45] Naomi Feldman: Typically yes. Model pins and rollouts are governed by your policy. Pins are config changes—audited.

[14:56] Priya Desai: Great.

[15:00] Greg Han: I have a more tactical question. Telemetry query latency. In incidents it gets worse. How do you make sure the bot response is not like 2 minutes.

[15:10] Dylan Brooks: We cap our response time. If queries exceed, say, 2–3 seconds, we return partial results and links. We also run a canary that monitors query latency.

[15:23] Greg Han: Good.

[15:26] Elena Markovic: Do you have an example audit event? Like actual fields.

[15:30] Kevin Osei: I can send a sample. Roughly: timestamp, actor (service identity / user), action, resource (service/env/tenant), scope used, request id, and outcome. And optionally “reason” for break-glass.

[15:50] Marcus Reed: Include retention and recommended review procedure. Like quarterly access review.

[15:55] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We’ll include that.

[16:00] Priya Desai: Another question: do you support SAML / SSO for the Console? And MFA requirements.

[16:07] Naomi Feldman: Yes, SSO/SAML and RBAC. For Private it’s generally integrated with your IdP.

[16:14] Elena Markovic: Ok.

[16:16] Nina Alvarez: What about data residency? We operate US and EU separately.

[16:21] Neha Kapoor: In Private, you can run separate deployments per region. That’s a common pattern.

[16:28] Greg Han: That increases operational overhead.

[16:30] Neha Kapoor: True, but we can standardize config and dashboards.

[16:35] Chloe Martin: The deep links and dashboards are parameterized by region, so it’s consistent.

[16:41] Elena Markovic: Alright. Can we talk failure modes? Like, what if your diagnostics service is down.

[16:48] Dylan Brooks: Then you still have raw dashboards and runbooks. The diagnostics service is not the only way to access metrics. Also, the bot degrades to “open these links” and stops trying to be smart.

[17:04] Greg Han: That’s acceptable.

[17:07] Priya Desai: And permissions if diagnostics service is compromised. Is there blast radius?

[17:13] Naomi Feldman: That’s why scopes are narrow and why we avoid giving it write permissions. Read-only, bounded.

[17:22] Marcus Reed: Plus audit.

[17:24] Naomi Feldman: Exactly.

[17:27] Elena Markovic: I want to ensure we can demonstrate to auditors: “bot cannot access customer prompts.” That’s a thing.

[17:36] Dylan Brooks: We don’t query prompts for diagnostics. It’s primarily metrics and config metadata. If you have logging for prompts, that’s separate and would be restricted.

[17:47] Priya Desai: Good.

[17:49] Greg Han: Last thing from me: we want “context completeness.” Like, did the incident record include deploy, config, saturation.

[17:57] Dylan Brooks: We track that as a score internally. We can expose it as a metric: which cards were present vs missing, and why missing.

[18:12] Greg Han: Great.

[18:14] Neha Kapoor: We’re at about halfway. Anything else you want to drill into? Maybe SLO exports.

[18:20] Elena Markovic: Yes. We need weekly executive reporting. Error budgets, incident counts. Can you do that without building a data warehouse.

[18:29] Chloe Martin: You can export snapshots. For private, some customers schedule an API pull that writes to their BI tool. We can do CSV/JSON exports.

[18:42] Marcus Reed: And those exports should be audited if it includes sensitive details.

[18:46] Kevin Osei: We can audit export actions.

[18:50] Priya Desai: Great.

[18:52] Nina Alvarez: Sorry, earlier you said “saturation signals include scheduler admission control.” Is that standard?

[18:58] Dylan Brooks: It’s a metric we like because it tells you the system is intentionally shedding load. It’s more actionable than just GPU util.

[19:08] Nina Alvarez: Makes sense.

[19:10] Elena Markovic: Okay. Next steps. I need artifacts. Audit event schema, SLO export format, and an architecture diagram with trust boundaries.

[19:22] Neha Kapoor: Yep. Kevin will send audit samples. Naomi will send security checklist. Chloe will send deep link examples and SLO export options. And then we’ll schedule a follow-up architecture review.

[19:40] Greg Han: And I’ll send our current SLO definitions and where we want them to land—Grafana and ServiceNow.

[19:46] Priya Desai: I’ll send the retention requirements and whether signing is required.

[19:51] Marcus Reed: I’ll send our separation-of-duties model.

[19:56] Neha Kapoor: Perfect.

[20:00] (crosstalk)

[20:01] Neha Kapoor: Any last questions?

[20:04] Elena Markovic: Not now. This was helpful.

[20:08] Neha Kapoor: Great, thanks everyone.
